# Calibration: when 0.8 really means 80% {#sec-ch03}

::: {.epigraph by="Lord Kelvin, 1883"}
When you can measure what you are speaking about, and express it in numbers, you know something about it.
:::

*"If a model says 80%, does that mean 80%?"* It sounds silly until it costs you money. Nothing in a model's maths forces its 0.8 to match reality. It matches only if the model was built well and *checked*, and even then it can drift. Checking is the most important habit in this book.

::: {.goals}
- Say what *calibrated* means, and why it differs from accurate.
- Check calibration with a reliability diagram and ECE.
- Fix a miscalibrated model, and check it group by group.
:::

## The weather forecaster's secret

In the 1970s, researchers checked American weather forecasters against what actually happened. When they said "30% chance of rain", it rained on about 30% of those days; when they said 70%, about 70% [@murphy1977]. Most people are nothing like this: ask for a range they're "90% sure" of, and they're right far less than 90% of the time.

Forecasters aren't good because they're always right. They're good because their numbers mean what they say.

![Two forecasters. For each thing they said ("30%", "70%" and so on), we count how often it actually happened. The careful forecaster sits on the diagonal: their 70% happens about 70% of the time. The overconfident one says 90% about things that happen only about 70% of the time.](/figures/ch04/forecasters.pdf){#fig-forecasters}

::: {.keyidea}
A model is calibrated when its 80% happens about 80% of the time.
:::

## Ranking is not calibration

A model's numbers can be good at two different things. **Ranking**: do attacks get higher numbers than harmless alerts? The **AUC** measures it: the chance a random attack scores above a random harmless alert (1 is perfect, 0.5 a coin toss). **Calibration**: when the model says 0.3, are three in ten of those alerts attacks?

![Two models, identical at ranking (same AUC) but not at calibration. Model A is the logistic regression from Chapter 2. Model B is the same model with its probabilities distorted: it still sorts the alerts in the same order, but its numbers no longer mean anything.](/figures/ch04/same-auc.pdf){#fig-same-auc}

Both models in @fig-same-auc have AUC {{< num ch04 lr.auc f3 >}}. Model B says 40% about alerts that are attacks only a few percent of the time. If you only sort, B is as good as A. The moment you put a threshold on its numbers or multiply them by a cost, it misleads you. Leaderboards report ranking scores; calibration is often not measured at all. For decisions, it's usually what matters most.

::: {.keyidea}
Ranking well and being calibrated are different skills; decisions need both.
:::

## How to check

Do what the weather researchers did. Take predictions where you know the outcome, group them by what the model said (0–10%, 10–20%…), and in each group compare the average prediction with how often it happened. Plotted, that's a **reliability diagram**: points on the diagonal mean the numbers can be trusted. Always look at how many cases sit in each group; a dot built on twelve alerts is weak evidence.

![The reliability diagram of our Chapter 2 model on alerts it never saw. Points on the dashed diagonal mean the model's numbers can be trusted as they are. Underneath, a histogram (log scale) shows how many alerts fall in each part of the range: most are near zero, and only a few are above 50%.](/figures/ch04/anatomy.pdf){#fig-anatomy-03}

For one number, use the **expected calibration error (ECE)**: the average gap between "said" and "happened", weighted by how many predictions each group holds [@naeini2015]. Our logistic regression's ECE is {{< num ch04 lr.ece f3 >}}, under one percentage point; Model B's is {{< num ch04 squashed.ece f2 >}}. But ECE is an average, so it can hide a badly calibrated corner, and the high end, where the dangerous cases are, is exactly such a corner.

## How calibration breaks, and how to fix it

**Rebalancing the data.** The most common cause, usually well meant. Attacks are rare ({{< num ch04 base pct >}}), so someone trains on a 50/50 mix "so the model sees more attacks". The ranking stays fine, but the model learns a world where attacks are common: its average prediction becomes {{< num ch04 bal_mean_pred pct >}}. Put a threshold on that and the team drowns.

**Overfitting** pushes probabilities towards 0 and 1. **Very large neural networks** tend to be overconfident [@guo2017]. And **the world changing**, say an attack campaign doubling the base rate, breaks a model that was calibrated last month.

![A model trained on 50/50 rebalanced data (red, solid line with squares) thinks attacks are about ten times more common than they are, and its probabilities sit far below the diagonal. After Platt scaling fitted on a separate calibration set (green, dashed line with circles), the same model is well calibrated again.](/figures/ch04/rebalanced.pdf){#fig-rebalanced}

The good news: a model that ranks well but is miscalibrated is usually easy to fix, without retraining. Keep back a **calibration set** it never trained on, and learn a small correction on top:

- **Platt scaling** fits a stretch and a shift on the model's log-odds [@platt1999]. The usual first choice.
- **Temperature scaling** fits one number that softens overconfident answers. The standard fix for neural networks.
- **Isotonic regression** fits any rising staircase [@zadrozny2002]. Flexible, but needs more data.

On the rebalanced model, Platt brings ECE from {{< num ch04 balanced.ece f3 >}} to {{< num ch04 fixes.Platt.ece f3 >}}. Temperature does nothing ({{< num ch04 fixes.Temperature.ece f3 >}}), and the reason is worth knowing: rebalancing didn't make the model *overconfident*, it *shifted* every prediction up. A temperature can only stretch around the middle.

![The three corrections, each fitted to the rebalanced model on the calibration set. Platt scaling learns an S-curve that can shift and stretch. Temperature scaling learns one number that only stretches around the middle, and here it barely changes anything. Isotonic regression learns any rising staircase.](/figures/ch04/fixes.pdf){#fig-fixes}

::: {.keyidea}
Temperature fixes overconfidence. It can't fix a wrong base rate.
:::

## Calibrated on average, wrong for one group

![Calibration checked separately for each alert source. Across all sources together, this model is well calibrated, with an ECE of about half a percentage point. But it overestimates the risk of DLP and Cloud alerts and underestimates EDR alerts, which really are more dangerous here. Averaging hides both mistakes.](/figures/ch04/by-source.pdf){#fig-by-source}

A model can be well calibrated overall and wrong for one group. Take a model that can't tell which system raised each alert. Overall ECE: an excellent {{< num ch04 generic.ece f3 >}}. But for alerts from laptops and servers it says {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.pred pct1 >}} when the truth is {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.actual pct1 >}}, and for data-leak alerts {{< num ch04 by_source.DLP.pred pct1 >}} when the truth is {{< num ch04 by_source.DLP.actual pct1 >}} (@fig-by-source). The errors cancel in the average, and the policy quietly closes real laptop attacks.

::: {.keyidea}
Check calibration inside every group you'll treat differently, not just on average.
:::

That means sources, customer tiers, languages, regions, and, when a model affects people's lives, groups of people.

::: {.breaks}
Calibration only holds for data like the data you measured it on, and it fades as tools, attackers and people change. And it says nothing about any single prediction: a perfectly calibrated 70% is still wrong three times in ten. Keep a fresh calibration set and recheck on a schedule.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Explain to a friend, with no technical words, the difference between a model that ranks well and one that's calibrated.
:::
